en: [2021:112] (1v1) (Success! Seal) Homage to the Three Jewels.

Having prostrated before him who has transcended the eight worldly dharmas and who is beyond the world, I compose this hymn of praise, which is esteemed by the noble ones and approved by the treatises.

Since the Sage consists of the three bodies, including the essential body together with its activity, there can be no praise from the very beginning without that [essential body]. Therefore, praise should begin with it.

For, because it is stated that "it is perfected as the *dharmadhātu*," it is intended to have the characteristic of the non-arising of the nature of all the Buddha-dharmas, which are pure in every aspect and free from outflows (*anāsrava*). Therefore, the *svābhāvikakāya* is, due to its identity with the emptiness of the non-arising of intrinsic nature, common to all Sugatas; thus, even the recitation of the *mahājñāna* and other qualities is well-established. [2021:113] Because it arises from the praise of the collection [of qualities], the *svābhāvikakāya* is considered the object of praise; the others [the *sambhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*] are not distinct from it, and they are based upon what has been said of it.
This fourfold hymn was composed by the teachers, through the distinction of the *Lakṣmīdhenu*, for the sake of awakening King Sātavāhana by means of a concise introduction.

[Commentary on Lokātītastava 1] Therein, the first verse begins with "Homage to you, O Transcendent One" (*lokātīta namas tubhyam*). "World" (*loka*) refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandhāḥ*). That which transcends this is the "Transcendent One" (*lokātīta*). As it is said in the *Abhidharma*: "What is existence? It is the five aggregates of clinging; and that is the world. Alternatively, by the word "world," the eight worldly dharmas—such as pleasure and pain, gain and loss—are expressed. Just as in the expression "the beds are crying," there is a metaphorical application of the term for the support (*āśraya*) to that which is supported (*āśrita*). Homage to you, the Transcendent One!

To what kind [of person]? To one who is *vivikta*, meaning empty (*śūnya*). Therefore, to the knower of gnosis (*jñānavedin*), that is, to one who has directly realized the gnosis of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*). Now, it may be granted that the very emptiness of the non-arising of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānutpāda-śūnyatā*) is the intrinsic nature of all Buddha-dharmas; nevertheless, how can that be directly realized here without reliance on a means (*upāya*)? If you say it is "Buddhahood" (*buddhatva*), this is not a fault. For it is said in the scripture: "The yoga of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā-yoga*) is indeed the means (*upāya*) for the compassionate self. It is for this very reason that he says:

“You who have long been weary out of compassion solely for the sake of the world’s welfare”: in this world, when harm has arisen, Buddhahood is the welfare; it is for that very purpose that you are weary. [The statement] “seeing the world suffering while one’s own mind is unarisen from the beginning” refers to being ignorant of welfare. Seeing [the world], you are weary out of compassion through the desire for its welfare, but not in a literal sense. For in the world, nothing desirable consists of pleasure or pain for the sake of producing weariness; rather, it is through sharing in the suffering of others. That welfare lasts as long as saṃsāra endures.

Alternatively, he remains "exhausted" because he is intent upon seeking the means to fulfill the intentions of every sentient being. For this very reason, regarding the Blessed One whose mind consists of compassion that has no other support, it is said: "All his outpourings are preceded by compassion and are purified by wisdom."
[Commentary on Lokātitastava 2] Now, one might object: "Could that which transcends the aggregates not be a sentient being, or perhaps a self? To this, he says:

"It is your view that there is no sentient being apart from the mere aggregates," and so forth. "The aggregates alone are the mere aggregates. As it is said: "There are only twelve factors of existence, which are the aggregates and the sense bases..."

"The elements—having reflected upon all these, no person (pudgala) is apprehended. From this scriptural statement, [it follows that] the world is merely that [collection of elements]. Your view is that apart from and distinct from those [elements], there is no being or person. Furthermore, even though the self does not exist, the designation "being" is applied to the aggregates themselves with reference to the notion of "I," [thinking] "I am the agent, I am the enjoyer. And for that purpose, O Great Sage, you have undergone supreme hardship.

Thus: "And for the sake of sentient beings" means for the purpose of establishing that all phenomena are selfless (*nirātmānaḥ*). The word *ca* (and) refers to the meaning of the previously mentioned word *khinna* (weary). By the word *kheda*, he indicates that you have undergone supreme weariness. Furthermore, for the sake of his beloved son, he indicates an excellence of vigor (*vīryātiśaya*), like a man who has entered a wilderness region of famine. "O Great Sage" (*mahāmune*): he is both great and a sage; or, because he surpasses the sages—that is, the Śrāvakas and others—he is the Great Sage (*mahāmuni*). According to the rule beginning with *pṛṣodarādi*, there is the substitution of *a* for the letter *ta*.

[Commentary on Lokātītastava 3] If this is so, then how is there no contradiction in addressing the Blessed One as "O Lokātīta, homage to you" when only the aggregates (*skandha*) exist? To this he says:
"O wise one, even those aggregates were revealed by you as being like an illusion, a mirage, a city of the Gandharvas, and a dream."

This is the summary of the meaning: they are like an illusion (*māyopama*) because they delude sentient beings by appearing as unreal objects; they are like a mirage (*marīcisannibha*) because they are devoid of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) due to the absence of distinct divisions; they are like a city of the Gandharvas (*gandharvanagaropama*) because they lack any basis other than a particular person (*pudgala*); and they are like a dream (*svapnopama*) because they are produced solely through the power of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) for the beautiful and so forth. O you of unsurpassed intelligence, these things have been revealed by you—devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)—to those who possess wisdom and are endowed with discernment. [Commentary on the *Lokātītastava* 4]

Now, one might ask: how can things that are established by their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and dependent upon causes and conditions (*hetupratyaya*) be without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)? To this, he says:
How indeed could those things which arise from causes and exist through their absence not be clearly considered equal to reflections?

But how can those things which are dependent upon causes and conditions be established by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? How could they be established by way of intrinsic nature? [2021:115] Since they are dependent upon those [causes and conditions], they are like reflections; being thus devoid of intrinsic nature, they are considered by you to be indeed without intrinsic nature. For this very reason they lack intrinsic nature: when the collection of causes and conditions exists, they arise; when that [collection] is absent, they do not arise. Being free from unity and plurality like a reflection, they are either non-deceptive, as he says, or [the text continues]: even in the *Śrāvaka-sūtra*...

Form is said to be like foam; sensation is like a bubble; perception is similar to a mirage; mental formations are like a plantain tree; and consciousness is declared by the Kinsman of the Sun to be like an illusion. (33) [Commentary on Lokātītastava 5] Furthermore, he demonstrates that each [of these] is individually unestablished in its own nature.
"How can that which consists of the elements (*bhūta*)—which are not graspable by the eye—be visual (*cākṣuṣa*)?

[This] shows the contradiction between the eye and the perception of form (*rūpa*). Since the eye does not have the elements as its object, how can that which consists of them—the derivative form (*bhautika-rūpa*)—be visual, graspable by the eye? Therefore, by you who speak thus, in asserting that [form] consists of earth and so forth without distinction, the grasping of form by the eye is refuted; and since that [grasping] is also [refuted] by the knowledge of that [truth], he says: "Form is not perceived apart from the causes of form. This is the meaning. Thus, in this [context].

[Commentary on Lokātītastava 6] Without that which is to be felt (*vedanīya*), there is no feeling; therefore, feeling is without self and lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). If it is argued, "When that which is to be felt exists, [feeling] will exist," then that too is "that which is to be felt. Since that object of feeling (*vedya*) is established by way of its own intrinsic nature, if it is argued, "The object of feeling will exist in dependence upon feeling," then even more so, in that case, the object of feeling does not exist through mutual dependence; this is what you intend. Therefore, he says: "That entity which is established in dependence upon something else is established in dependence upon that very thing."

[Commentary on *Lokātītastava* 7] If that which is to be depended upon is present, what is there for the dependent to depend upon? Because name (*saṃjñā*) and object (*artha*) are not different—because the designator (*abhidhāna*) and the designated (*abhidheya*) are non-distinct—the mouth would be burned by fire. If they were other, there would be no comprehension. You, the speaker of reality, the speaker of ultimate truth, have stated that if those two—the designated and the designator—were distinct and independent, then the existence or non-existence of the object in its own form [would follow].
[Commentary on Lokātītastava 8] You have stated that, from the perspective of conventional usage, both the agent and the action are independent.

Thus, the agent unconditioned by a Lord and so forth, as well as the action unconditioned [by an agent]—this too has been stated in two ways from the perspective of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), that is, merely by way of worldly convention. Why? Because the word "but" (*tu*) indicates that the establishment of these two—the agent and the action—is accepted only nominally (*nāmataḥ*).
[Commentary on *Lokātītastava* 9]

For this very reason, there is neither an agent nor an enjoyer. How then does conventional discourse proceed? It has been said: "Merit and demerit are born dependently. However, this dependent nature (*paratantra*) is not itself a substantially real entity. Why is this so? Because that which is dependently arisen has not been declared by you, O Lord of Speech, to exist by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). As it is said: "Those things which are dependently originated do not exist at all by way of intrinsic nature. [Commentary on *Lokātītastava* 10] Ignorance is not the object of knowledge, nor is consciousness possible without it.

Since establishment in this way depends upon a succession of others, therefore you have stated that knowledge and the object of knowledge do not exist by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). [Commentary on Lokātītastava 11]
If this is so, how is it that there is an exposition of the characteristics of the aggregates, such as "form has the characteristic of being subject to transformation"? To this he says:

"If the characteristic were different from the characterized, then that characterized would be without a characteristic. If they were not different, the non-existence of both would be clearly stated by you."

If that which is characterized by changeability (*rūpaṇa*) and so forth were distinct from the aggregates (*skandha*) such as form (*rūpa*), then form and the rest would be without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*). Alternatively, if there were no difference between the two, then in that case, what would be the characterized (*lakṣya*) and what the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)? Since their own-nature (*svarūpa*) is not perceived, how could the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the aggregates be established through the designation of the characterized and the characteristic?
[Commentary on *Lokātītastava* 12] For this very reason, you have seen this world with the eye of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).

Free from the characterized and the characteristic, devoid of verbal expression, it is peaceful because of the cessation of the proliferation of arising and so forth. As it has been said regarding a mirage: "A mirage appears like water, yet there is no water, nor anything else. The aggregates (*skandhas*) are likewise similar to a self; they are neither selves, nor do they exist in reality. To grasp at this world, which resembles a mirage, thinking "it exists," or even "it does not exist," is delusion (*moha*). When there is delusion, one is not liberated. [Commentary on *Lokātītastava* 13]

[2021:117] Having demonstrated the rejection of the attachment to the existence of entities consisting of the aggregates (skandha) that are designated dependently, he now offers praise by way of the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya):
"An entity does not arise as existent, nor as non-existent, nor as both existent and non-existent."
Thus he refutes the doctrine of the Satkāryavādins. He... [End of folio 5v] || [Colophon:
47r4–v4] The Commentary on the Catuḥstotra is completed. || ||
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.

In the year 38, while Nayapāla was residing at Kolipattana, this manuscript was written by the Buddhist Avadhūta, the venerable Bālabodha, for the sake of the Bhūṭānīya Locha Paṇḍita, the monk Śrī Vajradhvaja, in the Ṭeḍo Cave. It was written on the first day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, on a Monday, during the reign of the Emperor Śrī Jayabhīmadeva, who descended from the lineage of Raghu.
May there be auspiciousness! May the hosts of beings be devoted to the welfare of all the world. May peace prevail everywhere, and may the world become happy in every way. (Verse 45)

[2023:116] That entity which lacks an essence (*svabhāva*) is not produced, because it already exists. For being an effect (*kāryatā*) consists in dependence upon causes. What need is there for an existing entity that already exists to depend on a cause? As it has been said:
And how can that entity which is entirely free from all doubt depend [on anything]?

Nor is it non-existent; for "arising" is a property of what exists. How could it depend on what is non-existent? Because dependence is impossible for the non-existent. Thus it has been said: "The capacity of a cause exists when the effect is absent, not when it is present. Therefore, we do not maintain the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); for both existence and non-existence belong to those two [cause and effect]."

Thus, in reality, the effect would be entirely without a cause. Nor does that which is both existent and non-existent arise, because there is no such thing as a nature consisting of two contradictory properties. As it is said: "How could that which is both existent and non-existent be one? (Lokātītastava 13). Having refuted the existence of an effect-nature, he proceeds to negate the cause.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the negation of either one of cause and effect would entail the negation of both? How then can there be a negation by raising them individually? [Response: This is not a fault, because with respect to a real effect, even when that [effect] is not perceived, one superimposes the status of being a cause upon a mere entity (*vastumātra*)—that is, upon the application of conventional usage—and says to the world:
"How could it be produced neither from itself, nor from another, nor from both?"

Thus, for you who hold that the cause is of the nature of the effect, it would have to be of its own nature (*svarūpa*), of another nature (*pararūpa*), or of both natures. First of all, it does not arise from itself, because it does not exist as that very self-nature. Furthermore, what purpose would there be in its further production? How could there not be a contradiction in saying that "a self-nature is born from a self-nature"? Moreover, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasanga*) of an endless succession of births.

And consequently, because it is occupied with its own production, there is no opportunity for the production of another effect. Now, if it is argued that the cause itself becomes the effect, and thus the designation "it is born" refers merely to its manifestation—if this were so, there would be no fault regarding [the distinctions of] taste, potency, post-digestive transformation, power, color, and shape. Therefore, the claim that a non-cause becomes an effect does not logically support the sense of arising from itself (*svataḥ*). Nor does it arise from another (*parataḥ*), because [if it did], it would cease to be another. For "otherness" is only intended when there is a state of selfhood; it is like the mutual dependence between Caitra and Maitra. And it has been said:

Existence is traditionally held to be "other" only when it is established through its own nature by means of an external condition; if its own nature is not established, how can there be otherness from another, given that it is unestablished?

Thus, there is no establishment of self or other. Due to the absence of those two, the production of an effect from both is impossible. Therefore, it is established that nothing whatsoever arises from anything; how could it be known? Thus it is proven.
[Commentary on Lokātītastava 14] [Objection:

Surely destruction exists, because of the statement that "all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impermanent. Since that [destruction] exists, arising will also exist, and from that, stability as well; thus, everything is in order. [Reply: This is not so.
For destruction is not logically possible for that which exists and is endowed with stability.

And so forth. First of all, the destruction of that which exists—that is, of an entity possessing the property of persistence—is not tenable. Nor is it possible for that which does not exist—that is, for what lacks the property of persistence—to be destroyed; for how could there be destruction for something equal to a horse’s horn? In no way whatsoever. Alternatively, the opponent might ask: "How can that destruction be considered equal to a horse’s horn? Furthermore, even if destruction were to occur, it would be untenable in either case—whether it is distinct from or non-distinct from the entities themselves.
Destruction is neither different from the entity nor non-different from it. Why?
Because if it were a different entity, the entity would be eternal.

Nor would there be a relation such that "the entity or its destruction is not something other [than itself]. Alternatively, if the entity were empty of both, it would be inexpressible as either identical to or different from [itself]. To this he says:
[Commentary on Lokātītastava 16]
[2023:118] For if there were identity, the destruction of an entity would not be possible; for if there were difference, the destruction of an entity would not be possible.

The intention is that, in either case, there is simply no connection with existence (*bhāva*). That which cannot be expressed as being either identical to or different from [something else] is not connected with anything at all; for example, the son of a barren woman. And since the characteristic of impermanence is a property of real entities (*vastudharma*) that cannot be expressed as being either identical to or different [from them], this is a non-occurrence of the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddha-anutpanna-vyavahāra*). Nothing happens to it. If it is argued: "What then? It is simply that existence does not exist at all," [the response follows].

In that case, does the non-existence of an existing entity not occur, or does the non-existence of a non-existing entity occur? If the non-existence of an existing entity does not occur, how so? Or if the non-existence of a non-existing entity does not occur, how so? For you do not assert that the alteration of anything consists in the existence of its perception. Now, if it is said that the non-existence of an existing entity does not occur at all because of the non-persistence [of the entity] into a second moment;

If an entity’s intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) arises from its own cause, then because that state of being would be non-deviating, how could it become otherwise? It would be better if entities did not exist at all than for them to abandon their own non-existence. Furthermore:
if it were by nature stable in its own moment, why would it not endure for an eon? And if it were by nature unstable in its own moment, how could it possibly perish later?

Now, if it is argued that an entity arises with a nature that does not persist into the second moment due to its own cause, this is not so; for it is not logical that a property which is non-existent at that time can be the nature of an entity existing in the present.
When something exists by way of its own nature, it is not logical for it to be non-existent in that same manner.
How, then, could that which is not found [at that time] be its own nature? And that which does not exist—how could it be its own nature?
Furthermore:
"Since that which is unborn by its very nature, how could there be permanence or annihilation?

Because of this scriptural teaching, this conceptualization is not sound. To those, however, who think that the auxiliary conditions such as moisture—which assist the sprout and so forth—bring about a transformation of the seed but do not themselves produce the sprout, he says:

[Commentary on Lokātītastava 17] First of all, the arising of an effect from a cause that has perished is not tenable; nor is the arising from a cause that has not perished considered by you to be like a dream.

Thus, in both past and future states, there is no relationship of producer and produced, just as in the case of two rabbit horns. Nor is there such a relationship between two things that have not yet perished, which would be equivalent to the left horn of a cow. Therefore, your notion of arising is considered to be like the birth of a maiden from sleep. If so, how is it stated—?

"There are four conditions: the causal condition (*hetu*), the objective condition (*ālambana*), the immediate condition (*anantara*), and likewise the dominant condition (*adhipateya*). There is no fifth condition.
In this regard, it is held that from the seed alone there is an immediate destruction, and thus the immediate [seed] is the condition for the sprout and so forth.
[Commentary on Lokātītastava 18 & 19]

If it is argued that because its remaining together with its own cause, the seed, is contradictory, the sprout arises while destroying the seed—then [we reply]: destruction occurs while [the entity] exists. Since they would exist simultaneously, how could there be destruction? Alternatively, if [destruction occurs] when [the entity] already exists, that same fault applies; thus, it is not tenable. For whether that which arises is existent or non-existent, since arising is negated in both cases, both eternalism and nihilism are established. Therefore...
All arising whatsoever is said by you, who propound mere conditionality (*pratyayatāmātra*), to be like the arising of an illusion (*māyotpāda*).
For an sprout does not arise from a seed that has already ceased, nor from one that has not yet ceased.
Therefore, you maintain that this world arises from conceptual construction (*parikalpa*)—that is, it arises from nothing but ignorance (*avidyā*).
It has been fully understood that [the world] is non-existent and false; for this very reason, it is unarisen and does not perish.

Since it is unarisen by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it does not perish, like the water in a mirage. As it is said: "Neither destroyed nor arisen, equal to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), you demonstrate the seven elements; this is your conformity with the world. Now, he shows praise for the refutation of the Sarvāstivāda doctrine: "Granted, let there be no destruction of the aggregates; rather, let there be a transition through the three times. He refutes that [position]. (Commentary on *Lokātītastava* 20)

There is no transmigration for that which is eternal, nor is there transmigration for that which is impermanent. [It is said: "Transmigration belongs to the five aggregates. Indeed, past aggregates, as well as those of the future and the present, possess designations [such as "past," etc.]. However, the proponents of the existence of all things (*sarvāstivādins*), who maintain the theory of the transition through the three time-periods, do not [assert this] because of [the fact that] destruction [would otherwise occur]. In that regard, for an entity that is eternal and does not abandon its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there is no transmigration—that is, no reconnection with another state of existence. For by that same nature through which it exists in the present, it did not exist in the past; and by that same nature through which it existed in the past, it does not exist in the present.

How, then, could there be the transition of that [self] by way of that [self], or the establishment of the three time periods? Nor is there the going and coming to another state of existence for that which is impermanent, because the previous five aggregates perish without leaving a trace (*niranvaya-vināśāt*). Since something entirely new arises and emerges immediately after the destruction without a trace, there is no transmigration or transition for either of the two. Yet, it is not as if there is no saṃsāra, O monks, nor is there no going and coming to another state of existence. How, then, does one transmigrate therein? He says:
O best among the knowers of reality, you have declared that cyclic existence is like a dream.

As for what the Elder said: "Just as a reflection is transferred into a clear mirror, so too, O fool, the world of people thinks 'it is happiness. But surely there is no transfer of that [reflection] there, nor does it exist without that [mirror]. In the same way, the transition of the aggregates (*skandha*) into another existence would occur; however, this non-transfer is to be understood by the wise in every respect, just as in dreams. And just as they move from one country to another, from one village to another house, and so forth—how is this so? To this he says:
[Commentary on Lokātītastava 21] Logicians maintain that suffering is self-caused, caused by another, caused by both, or without cause; but you have declared it to be dependently arisen.

The meaning is that this is merely a conventional designation (*dharmasaṃketa*), established without analysis, consisting of mere worldly usage (*vyavahāramātra*), such that "having attained this, it is produced. If so, how and for whom is it said that its lack of production by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānutpāda*) is emptiness (*śūnyatā*)? To explain precisely how this is so, he says:
"That which is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), that very thing you consider to be emptiness. [Commentary on the *Lokātītastava* 22]
"An independent entity does not exist"—this is your incomparable lion’s roar.

By teaching the two truths (*satyadvaya*), you demonstrate the praise of the Dharma. [The verse says: "That which is dependent origination, arising through conditions internal and external—that very emptiness of dependence is your doctrine. Based on dependent origination, the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) is declared by your wisdom; indeed, dependent origination itself is the emptiness of intrinsic nature. How so? An independent entity does not exist.

Because there is no entity established by way of its own nature (*svabhāva*) that is dependent upon causes and conditions. If it is argued, "Surely [an entity] will be established as having its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) while being dependent upon causes and conditions," [the response is: How can that which is dependent on another be something produced? That which is produced is artificial; how, then, could it be called "established by way of its own nature"? As it is said: "How indeed could there be a so-called 'own-nature' that is produced? Furthermore: "O Lion’s Roar, you are incomparable" (*atula*), meaning you are beyond all comparison.

The uncommon lion’s roar is dependent origination and emptiness. As it is said: “That which is cause, condition, karma, and the experience of its maturation—all that is empty of intrinsic nature. This is your powerful lion’s roar. “Powerful” means possessing strength, being unassailable. As it is said: “Seeing this conditionality and the lack of intrinsic nature in the world, one should see that emptiness is designated in dependence upon this.
There is no cause and no fruit; there is no other ‘sentient being’ here at all in the entire world. [2023:121]

[Commentary on Lokātītastava 23] If it be so, let the world be empty of duality, lacking intrinsic nature, and dependent; yet you say it is not so: "The teaching of the nectar of emptiness is for the sake of abandoning all conceptual constructions; whoever has a grasping even toward that, he has been refuted by you."

For one who has wrongly grasped the teaching on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), there arises an attachment even to that [emptiness], because of the perception of emptiness as a real entity; thus, you have been censured for this wrong grasp. As it was said: "Kāśyapa, those who perceive emptiness and thereby resort to emptiness—I say that they are utterly ruined. From this scriptural authority, your teaching of emptiness, which has emerged from the ocean of the Word, is a nectar-like instruction intended for the abandonment and relinquishing of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, the person who is deeply attached to emptiness as an intrinsic nature has been refuted. And so it was said: "Emptiness itself would become an entity if the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) were not overcome. When both are empty through emptiness, what talk can there be regarding mere awakening?
[Commentary on *Lokātītastava* 24] For this reason:
"O Protector, you have revealed that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature—inactive, powerless, empty, like an illusion, and arising from conditions. (11v3)

Strivings (*īhā*)—whether of body or speech—do not exist among those internal phenomena (*adhyātmika-dharma*) which are devoid of striving; they are "strivingless" (*nirīha*) because of the departure of striving. They are "insubstantial" (*vaśika*) and "vain" (*tuccha*) because they are empty (*śūnya*). "Strivingless," "insubstantial," and "vain"—this is the meaning. Precisely because they are dissociated from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are "empty. How then are they dependent (*paratantra*)? Like an illusion, they arise without [independent] conditions. Therefore, O Lord, you have revealed them to be without intrinsic nature. And so it has been said:

"All phenomena are like an illusion for people; they are empty by nature, just as the sky is. Those who understand this very nature cross over [samsara] and do not cling anywhere. This is the Samādhi of the Equality of All Phenomena (*sarvadharma-samatā-samādhi*). Whose is it? It belongs to one who has abandoned affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and so forth, even while speaking of them. Or rather, it is the arising of the Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*) for those who are pure. [Commentary on Lokātītastava 25] As he said accordingly:
"Nothing whatsoever has been produced by you, nor has anything whatsoever been ceased—neither purification nor defilement. Rather, as it was before, so it is after; you have awakened to suchness."

Just as previously, because the afflictions (*saṃkleśa*) are by nature *tathatā*—being devoid of falsity and non-existent—there is non-arising (*anutpādatā*); so too, later, in the state of purification (*vyavadāna*), because of the non-differentiation of the *dharmadhātu*, you have realized that *tathatā* which is neither prior nor posterior. For what reason? Not otherwise, because both are without intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatva*). As it is said: "O Lord, for one who knows you, conceptual constructions (*saṃkalpa*) do not arise at any time; for these two states are merely conceptual construction, and thus they are equal to cyclic existence (*bhava*). (2023:122)
Regarding this, it is said:
"For without having attained this cultivation (bhāvanā) which is not practiced by the Noble Ones,
consciousness here never becomes signless (animitta) in any way whatsoever."

※※※※※※※※※※※ This [reality], which is like the illusion of the world, is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and is not accessible through conceptualization; it is described as being free from discursive thought (*avitarka-avicāra*). Why is it that it is practiced by the Noble Ones (*ārya*) with reverence, continuously and for a long time? Because consciousness (*vijñāna*) does not become "signless" (*animitta*) here [in the absence of such practice]. The "sign" (*nimitta*) consists of ignorance (*avidyā*) and formative forces (*saṃskāra*). It is the cause of consciousness, which is the seed of existence (*bhava*). Through separation from that [cause], consciousness becomes signless here in the Mahāyāna, according to the teaching on the cultivation of the Noble Path; it is certainly not the case otherwise. Therefore, it is said: "Likewise, the sign [is absent] due to the separation from its cause."
[Commentary on Lokātītastava 27] To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"There is no liberation without resorting to the signless (*animitta*)," as you have stated. This is what the Blessed One said: "The single truth is non-arising (*anutpāda*), which is my very self."

Therefore, in the Mahāyāna, that [is taught] as "signless" (*animitta*). This means that it has been taught and revealed in its entirety and in detail that all phenomena (*sarvadharmāḥ*) are by nature devoid of the essence of arising (27cd). And thus it is said: "Since the object of knowledge is not established in any way whatsoever, even the non-conceptual cognition does not reach that [object]; the wise know reality (*tattva*) to be of such a kind. (13r1) *Note: The term *nirālasvaṃ* appears to be a corruption; based on the context and the Sanskrit provided, it likely intends *nirālambanaṃ* (without an objective support).*
[Commentary on Lokātītastava 28] Whatever merit has been acquired by me through praising you, the recipient of praise, may that merit— free from the bonds of causal signs— overflow like the ocean.
May the entire world be freed from the bondage known as afflictions and karma, or rather, may it be free from that sign which is the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).

Thus: (28cd). The intrinsic nature (*svābhāvikakāya*) is common to all Sugatas; it has the characteristic of the non-arising of the intrinsic nature of all Buddha-qualities, and the Blessed One consists of the *dharmadhātu* and transcends the world. His praise is common [to all], being produced according to the method of the two-fold [classification]. Immediately after that, the three bodies (*trikāya*) are praised specifically; then, the Sage is presented through the distinction of his aspects. Among these, first is the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), immediately after that the Enjoyment Body (*sambhogakāya*), and then the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*). This very point will be explained here.

O Great Sage, you are inconceivable in terms of birth, dharma, and body; thus it has been said: "On the full moon day of the month of Vaiśākha, on the island of Śāntadvīpa, we shall strike the pit of the crocodile, the king of thirst, with the weapon of peace. (End of the commentary on the *Lokātītastava*)
Thus he said:

"The Tathāgata is eternally of the nature of non-arising; all phenomena are similar to the Sugata. Yet, by grasping at signs, those of childish intellect wander among phenomena that are non-existent in this world. For the Tathāgata is the reflection of wholesome, untainted phenomena. Therein, neither 'thus' nor 'not thus' exists, yet his image is seen throughout the entire world—this being due to the mere conditionality of things."
The meaning is: "of the reflection of the Tathāgata.

Therefore, he demonstrates the praise of the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which is the domain of ordinary practitioners and worldlings: "O Peerless One, homage to you, the knower of the reality that is devoid of intrinsic nature, who are intent on the welfare of this world that is ruined by false views. (1ab, 2cd)

Thus: "O you who have transcended comparison, homage to you, O knower of the absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva). The path is without intrinsic nature. That which is sought is the goal (artha), namely the fruit called Buddhahood. He whose nature (svabhāva) is the realization of both of these—the state of supramundane cause and fruit—is the "knower of the goal that is without intrinsic nature. Homage to him!

How is it so from the perspective of conventional truth? You are one who acts for the benefit of this world that is ruined by views—that is, ruined by the false vision of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the like, fallen into ruin, and rendered destitute; furthermore, you act for the benefit of those situated in Buddha-fields devoid of Buddhas, who are ignorant of the true path. This is because you teach the path in which all phenomena are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Moreover, by manifesting your own birth and so forth—just like a conjured elephant—you bring about the welfare of the world.
It has been stated that, in the future, Buddhahood will arise for them, and thus they have been delivered from that [suffering].

Now, one might ask: "How can the path be without intrinsic nature? To this he says: "And indeed, nothing at all was seen by you with the Buddha-eye" (2ab). The word *ca* means "because. At the time of perfect awakening (*abhisambodhi*), indeed, not even the slightest thing established by way of intrinsic nature was seen or perceived by you with the Buddha-eye. "Buddha" refers to the Buddha-nature; just as Bhīmasena is called Bhīma. This belongs to him, thus it is the "Buddha-eye. By that [eye], which is the eye of wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya-prajñā-cakṣus*).
And your vision, O Protector, is unsurpassed, seeing the reality of the ultimate meaning. (2cd)

And here too, the word *ca* means "therefore. There is no superior (*anuttara*) [to it]; because there is nothing superior (*uttara*)—that is, more excellent—than this, it is *anuttara*. It is your vision (*dṛṣṭi*), which sees the true reality (*tattvārtha*). It is that which sees the actual reality and realizes it directly. Regarding the statement "the awakening (*abhisambodhi*) is the non-arising and non-ceasing of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*)," and that this is "unsurpassed perfect awakening" (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*): if this is so, one might ask, "How is it unsurpassed if the intellect functions in the form of a distinction between what is to be awakened to and what awakens? To this he says:

From the perspective of ultimate reality, there is neither a knower nor anything to be known here. (3ab) The particle *ca* is used for emphasis; thus, there is no knower whatsoever—neither a self (*ātman*) nor anything else—and furthermore, there is nothing to be known, whether external or internal, here from the perspective of ultimate reality. This refers to the realization of things as they truly are.

"Aho! You have awakened to the nature of reality that is most difficult to understand" (3cd). "Aho" expresses wonder. O Protector, you have awakened to the nature of reality that is most difficult to understand—namely, the emptiness of the non-arising of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena. As it is said: "Behold the internal as empty; behold the external as empty. Nothing whatsoever exists. Even he who meditates upon that emptiness [is affected]. For there is the statement: "Even when clarity is present, if perception arises, the mind becomes a target for the afflictions."

If there is no apprehension of either [the self or phenomena] as empty, how then is there the arising of the untainted, unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), as well as the cessation of affliction? To this he says:
"But not a single dharma has been produced by you, nor has any been ceased. Rather, through the very vision of equality, the unsurpassed state has been attained. (4cd)

Through the vision of the equality of the non-arising of all phenomena, there is also the equality of affliction and purification. Therefore, the state attained by that vision is the unsurpassed; "attained" means realized, and "the unsurpassed state" refers to Buddhahood, which is the nature of non-abiding nirvāṇa. [Objection: Well then, how is Buddhahood—the nirvāṇa distinguished from saṃsāra—unsurpassed? [Reply: It is said: "Nirvāṇa was not sought by you through the removal of saṃsāra. (5ab)

"O Protector, peace has been attained by you through the non-apprehension of saṃsāra. (5cd) "Not by the removal of saṃsāra": the designation "saṃsāra" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and birth—namely, the twelve links of existence (*bhavāṅga*). There is no removal, elimination, or casting out of these; rather, by that [non-apprehension], Nirvāṇa—that is, Buddhahood—was sought and desired by you for the sake of delivering the world. How was Nirvāṇa attained? He says: "O Protector, peace has been attained by you through the non-apprehension of saṃsāra. This means that by not perceiving saṃsāra as a real entity, peace was realized.

Because the intrinsic nature of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is not perceived, as it has been said: "Behold existence as consisting of illusion; the world does not consist of twelve links. Arisen from mutual causes, one does not know what is equal or supreme. Nevertheless, how can there be a unity of these two mutually contradictory things? To this he says:
"You have realized the single flavor of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*). (6ab)

You have realized the single flavor (*ekarasa*) [of all things]; for the teaching states that the one truth is called "non-arising" (*anutpāda*). This refers to the single flavor of non-arising and suchness (*tathatā*) in both affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*), that is, in *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa*.
How is it that you are pure in every respect because of the indivisibility of the *dharmadhātu*? (6cd)

"Because of the non-distinction of the *dharmadhātu*" means that there is no distinction between the two, as they are both alike in the non-arising and non-distinction of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Just as *nirvāṇa* is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), so too is the world (*loka*). As it is said: "Since for both there is neither coming nor going, and no abiding characterized by them, what difference could there be in reality between the world and *nirvāṇa*? Therefore, "you are pure in every respect. This is because you are pure from the very beginning (*yādāvera*) and, finally, "in every respect" means from everything.

[This is explained] from the beginning of the roots of the latencies of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*) up to their limit. As it is said: "The realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is unestablished; its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not exist. If it is asked how these two are taught as distinct, he says:
"O Lord, not even a single syllable was produced by you, yet the entire assembly of those to be trained was satisfied by the rain of Dharma. (7ab–7cd)

O Lord, not even a single syllable has been produced by you, because the two [the teacher and the taught] are distinct [only conventionally], owing to their having the *dharmadhātu* as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). As it is said: "The *dharmadhātu* is unproduced; within it, the mind arises. How can the movement of syllables be sought therein? [Yet] the intellect [perceives it]. Furthermore, the entire assembly of those to be trained (*vaineyajana*) has been satiated by the rain of Dharma. The word "entire" (*kṛtsna*) includes the sense of the word "again" (*punaḥ*).

By him, the entire assembly of those to be trained was satisfied with the rain of Dharma according to their inclinations and in accordance with their spiritual lineages (gotra). This is because he possesses the speech that gathers the assembly of those to be trained through the indivisibility of abstaining from false speech. [An objection is raised: "Surely, how can there be the satisfaction of those to be trained by the rain of Dharma without the appropriation of the aggregates (skandha)? Furthermore, how can there be speech that transcends the world if there is no such appropriation? To this, he says: [2024:109]
You have no power over the aggregates, the elements, or the sense-bases; your mind is equal to space, having emerged from all phenomena.

Regarding the aggregates and so forth, which resemble reflections and the like, you have no power of attachment, just as in the case of a magical person (*māyāpuruṣa*), because you are free from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Therefore, your mind is equal to space. This is because of the statement that "space, the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and awakening are characterized by non-duality. Thus, you have "emerged from all phenomena" (*sarvadharmmeṣu niḥsṛtaḥ*)—that is, from all internal and external phenomena. [Question: How is it that the Blessed One’s teaching is not "unestablished," given that it takes into account sentient beings of inferior, middling, and superior capacities?
By the power of their own mental resolve (*svādhimokṣa*), they conceptualize everything in such and such a way, like a reflection in a mirror. As it is said:
"Therefore, the notion of a sentient being (*sattvasaṃjñā*) does not arise for them in any way whatsoever. (9ab)

In every respect, there is no [logical] alternative for you, because all other conceptual constructions have ceased; for it is said: "Moreover, toward sentient beings afflicted by suffering, you are exceedingly compassionate" (9cd).

Because of the state of constant flux through arising, ceasing, and suffering, the aggregates (*skandhas*) of those wandering in *saṃsāra* are suffering. You are exceedingly compassionate toward those beings afflicted by them; you consist of compassion. The word "and" (*ca*) [in the verse] has the sense of an implicit conjunction (*anuktasamuccayārtha*). Therefore, there is no contradiction in the fact that even while remaining in a body consisting solely of *dharmas*, your activity is most inconceivable, being projected by the merits and specific aspirations of people.

Now, if it is said that "the aggregates of one in cyclic existence are suffering," then the five supramundane aggregates—morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—which consist of untainted bliss, would appear [to be suffering as well]. And so it has been said: "That is bliss where there is cessation; therefore, there is relinquishing and taking up of the mundane and the supramundane.

To this, he replies: "O Lord, regarding pleasure and pain, self and selflessness, permanence and impermanence, and so forth—in these various conceptual constructions, your intellect does not become attached. (10ab–cd)

Bodily pleasant feeling is merely the counteraction of suffering; that which consists of perception is purely mental, being constructed by conceptualization. Thus, your intellect does not become attached to the various conceptual constructions such as pleasure and so forth, nor does any doubt arise here, because there is an absence of an intrinsic nature in things such as pleasure that would exist as real entities, and because the aggregate of feeling has been refuted. Furthermore, since the Great Sage has warded off the views concerning self and non-self, even that conceptual construction does not exist.
Therefore, he says: "The range of speech has ceased; the range of the mind has ceased. For the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is indeed unarisen and unceasing, like nirvāṇa.
If this is so, how did the Lord of Tuṣita take up the womb? To this he says: [2024:110]
It is your conviction that there is no going and no coming of phenomena whatsoever; (11ab) there is no state of being a heap anywhere; therefore, you are a knower of the ultimate truth. (11cd)

But here there is no coming from Tuṣita, nor even the conceptualization of seeing the parinirvāṇa; for the world, there is no end or limit anywhere, nor is there any state of being a heap here. Some read "piṇḍo vā skandhabhāva" instead. The word "iti" means "because. It is your view that there is neither going nor coming of any phenomena (*dharmas*). Your wisdom (*prajñā*) consists in the determination of the true nature of reality.

Therefore, there is no state of being a "heap" of phenomena anywhere in such things as the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) imagined by the Sāṃkhyas and others. In this regard, you are a knower of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), a knower of the unconditioned reality, and—moreover—a knower of the meaning of the non-arising of all phenomena; for it is said: "The Tathāgata is eternally of the nature of non-arising.
"You are omnipresent, yet you are not born anywhere. (12ab)

And you are omnipresent, because of your nature of non-arising; yet you are not born anywhere. Furthermore, in ultimate reality, you have not arisen in any place, at any time, or from causes and conditions.
Because you possess a body of dharmas that is beyond birth, you are inconceivable, O Great Sage. (12cd)
The birth-body consists of the enjoyment-body and the emanation-body; the dharma-body is the suchness [of these two], which is inconceivable and beyond the sphere of perception. Why?
Because the world is devoid of unity and difference, like an echo. You, the blameless one, have realized that it is free from transition and destruction. (13ab–cd)
O Lord, you have realized that cyclic existence is eternal yet free from annihilation, devoid of both the characterized and the characteristics, and like a dream or an illusion.

By such statements as "it does not exist now, having not existed before," [the Buddha taught] that the world is free from eternalism and nihilism. Because it does not remain for even a single moment, it is devoid of transition and destruction; there is neither one who transmigrates nor a process of transmigration, neither arising nor ceasing. Since both are mutually dependent like agent and action, both are unestablished by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Thus, you have awakened to this irreproachable truth.

[This is] through the abandonment of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable (*kleśajñeyāvaraṇa*). If it is asked how this is so, it is because: "O Lord, you have understood cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) to be like a dream, an illusion, and so forth; you have known it to be unarisen by nature (*svabhāvānutpanna*). Therefore, you are beyond reproach, as you have said: 'Just as those who are asleep wander through various countries, villages, and houses in dreams via improper bodily paths, coming and going upon those paths, so too does the world [wander] among the five destinies (*pañcagati*')."

What was accomplished by that realization? Because of the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-anupalambha*), O sinless one, those afflictions (*kleśa*) whose root and limit are the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) have been conquered by you. Those for which the latent predisposition alone is the root cause and the limit—that is, the final boundary—are "those whose root and limit are the latent predispositions. O sinless one, those afflictions have been conquered; they have been eliminated. Therefore, it was said: "When there is a basis (*āśraya*), both passion (*rāga*) and dispassion (*virāga*) arise. How were they eliminated? Because, O sinless one, the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*) has been acquired by you through the very nature of the afflictions.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Alternatively, by the word "affliction," ignorance is meant; its intrinsic nature is improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), and the intrinsic nature of that [attention] is also ignorance. Furthermore, because of the statement, "The wise say that the establishment of another's wealth is either established or unestablished," here "intrinsic nature" refers to non-establishment, which is non-arising. And according to one position, it is "from the very nature of the afflictions"; furthermore, it is called "ignorance" because of the statement, "due to its being non-existent."

It indicates that ignorance (*avidyā*) has a nature that does not exist; by the word "and" (*ca*), it is [meant] from the perspective of the nature of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Indeed, because ignorance—the cause of the afflictions—does not arise, you have acquired the deathless (*amṛta*) and attained *nirvāṇa*. Or rather, the nature of the afflictions is the non-arising of intrinsic being (*svabhāva*); it is for that very reason, and not through the destruction of the intrinsic characteristic-nature of the afflictions. Or again, "from the nature of the afflictions" means: the nature of the afflictions is their intrinsic being (*svabhāva*); from that [nature].

He does not abide in the afflictions, nor in sense objects, nor even in the collection of the sense faculties, nor does he stand amidst obstacles; thus, he is indeed non-abiding. Yet, this is not due to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*). Alternatively, its nature is the cause, which is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and that is merely that—this is the meaning. As it is said: "O Desire, I know your root; you are born, they say, from conceptual construction," and so forth. [The phrase] "is fully understood" now shows the essential nature of the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*): "O Wise One, you have seen form as being without characteristics, like a formless thing. (16ab)

Form has been seen by you as being without form, like space, characterized by the nature of transformation (*rūpaṇā*), because of the impossibility of identity or difference between the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the object characterized (*lakṣya*). You are a hero due to your victory over the four Māras; nevertheless, you are seen by me within the sphere of form (*rūpagocara*) with limbs radiant with the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).

For when a person to be trained has as their object of perception merely form (*rūpa*), it is said: "The foolish are attached to forms; those who are middling attain detachment from them; those who know its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and possess pure intellect are liberated from form. Is it not the case that for the Blessed One, the very seeing of form is right seeing (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), and that this is also the case for the Noble Ones (*ārya*), and not only for the foolish? Regarding the word "furthermore" (*param*) and so forth:
"One is not called 'one who has seen' simply because form has been seen" (17ab).

The word "ca" has the sense of "because. Because you are not correctly seen by means of form—that is, by form alone—by the Noble Ones (*ārya*), since the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form is not established [as ultimately real]. To the question "How even by the Noble Ones? he says: "When the Dharma is seen, you are well-seen; yet dharmatā is not seen. (17cd)

Seeing this conditionality (*idaṃpratyayatā*), one perceives only phenomena (*dharma*). Perceiving phenomena, one does not perceive [a self-]substance (*artha*), because of the statement: "The Victors are the Dharma-body. Therefore, when the Noble Ones have seen the Dharma, you have been well-seen; you have been correctly seen, because there is nothing further to be seen. How then is it that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is not seen? True; the nature of phenomena, which is the non-arising of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānutpāda*), is indeed not seen at all. If it is asked: "In that case, how is there the vision of the Blessed One?"

Because of the statement that "the Tathāgata is eternally of the nature of non-arising," the cognition that takes him as its object conforms to his form. At that time, what [object] is seen by which [subject], since the cognition is itself unarisen? Thus, in its true sense, non-seeing alone is right seeing. As it is said: "The Tathāgata is indeed a reflection of wholesome, untainted phenomena; yet herein there is neither suchness nor a Tathāgata, and yet an image is perceived throughout the entire world."

The established position is that the Blessed One’s vision is precisely the vision of the non-arising of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, he said: “There is no solidity in your body; there is neither flesh, bone, nor blood. (18ab) Through visible [objects] and the merit of cognition, [your body appears] like a reflection in a mirror. For this very reason, you have shown your body in space like a rainbow. (18cd) There is no sickness or atoms in your body, nor is there the occurrence of hunger or thirst. (19ab)

By you, for the sake of conforming to the world, worldly activity was demonstrated. (19cd) O Sinless One, there is no fault of karmic obscuration in you in any way whatsoever. (50ab) By you, out of compassion for the world, the overflowing of karma was displayed.
(20cd) [It was done] by you, out of compassion for the world, so that the world might indeed have conviction in the fruit of karma.
The praise of ritual action has been demonstrated [in the case of] the *khadira* wood splinters and so forth;
likewise [at 2024:113].
"O Lord, because there is no differentiation in the *dharmadhātu*, there is no differentiation of vehicles;

for the wise, the vehicle that is the wealth for the benefit of others is indeed one alone. As for the threefold vehicle that was taught by you, it was [taught] according to the means of entry for sentient beings."

"For the sake of introducing individuals belonging to the lineage of the Śrāvakas," [it is said that] the vehicles of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas have been proclaimed and taught. As it was said: "No one knows the Buddha, nor the nature (*dharmatā*) of the Buddhas; if he did not conform to the world, he would not be a guide for the world in this world. [Objection: Granted that there may be a distinction of vehicles (*yāna*) due to the distinctions among Śrāvakas and others, but how can there be a distinction of bodies (*kāya*), given that the *dharmadhātu* is undifferentiated? [Reply: True. However, even though [the Buddha] is one, there is a distinction made by way of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) in consideration of those to be trained (*vineyajana*). It is with reference to its essential nature (*svarūpa*) that he says:
O Jina, your body is eternal, stable, auspicious, and composed of Dharma.

(22ab) It is eternal because, like a forest fire, it never ceases to burn away the fuel of the afflictions of those to be trained; it is stable because the Enjoyment Body (sāmbhogika-kāya) is seen by those free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) as never returning [to saṃsāra]; it is auspicious because the Dharma Body (dharmakāya) is here perfectly pacified through the burning of the dry fuel of all phenomena and objects of knowledge, being tranquil and beyond conceptual elaboration; and it is composed of Dharma because there is no differentiation within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). O Conqueror, O Victor over all grasping, every body of yours has the nature of reality (*dharmatā-svabhāva*). For indeed, such is...

And for the sake of those to be trained (*vineyajana*), you have demonstrated cessation (*nivṛtti*). Because of the absence of those to be trained in your presence, and furthermore for the sake of the realization of those to be trained through scripture (*āgama*), you have again demonstrated cessation; yet not by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpataḥ*). As it is said:

"Do you not indeed enter final nirvāṇa through the enjoyment body (*sāmbhogikakāya*) and the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*)? Nor does the Dharma disappear; for the Body of the Nature of Reality (*tathatātmadharmatākāya*) manifests nirvāṇa within the body that brings sentient beings to the further shore."
For this very reason,
you are beheld again by those devoted to you throughout the innumerable world-systems.

"By those who long for death, birth, perfect awakening, the turning of the wheel [of Dharma], and nirvāṇa" (23cd)—that is, by those who are greedy for their own mental convictions (*svādhimokṣa*). Therefore, by the power of their own mental convictions, fools imagine everything in such and such ways; they do not understand that the conduct of the Perfectly Awakened One belongs to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). He says exactly this:
"O Protector, you have no conceit, no conceptual construction, and no movement" (24ab).

The conformity [to others] is the consideration of the world’s disposition. This is not a conceptual construction such as "does he have another disposition or not? nor is it "he does not. It is the recollection of the investigation of the deluded. How is there teaching by the Blessed One in the accomplishment of the welfare of others? He says: "Without effort, your buddha-activity proceeds in the world. (24cd)

Without effort, your activity as a Buddha proceeds in the world among those of the lineage to be trained, never overstepping them, like the rays of an arrow released with force. Because it is impelled by former vows, it is effortless; thus, it issues forth at will even from walls and other such places, according to the statement:
"In all places. Everything is indeed well-established, even in the presence of contradictory ornaments.

"Thus, having scattered flowers of inconceivable and immeasurable qualities over the Sugata, whatever merit has been acquired by me—by that, may sentient beings here become partakers of the most profound Dharma of the Sage.

This is the abiding of the *nirmāṇakāya*. The term "Sugata" is endowed with a threefold meaning: he is the Sugata because he has transcended the sphere of anxiety regarding himself and others; he is "inconceivable" (*acintya*) because he is beyond the range of inference; and he is "immeasurable" (*aprameya*). This is because of the statement: "There is the profundity of the Dharma of emptiness, and the other [qualities] are its vastness."

Having scattered flowers of profound and sublime virtues and offered praise, I have performed this [act]. May the merit acquired here in this world through skill in faith and wisdom cause sentient beings to partake in the most profound Dharma of the Lord of Munis. For it is said: "The non-arising and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is supremely profound; those who see emptiness are bewildered by it. Thus, may they partake in that Dharma of the Lord of Munis.
The Commentary on the Praise of the Nirmāṇakāya. || O ||
